1.title: Dance does not begin in the studio
1.description: Before we begin exploring technique, musicality, interaction, and variability, I suggest looking a little deeper. Most of us come to tango with a body that is already formed. We carry years of habits, work, stress, sport, or a sedentary lifestyle behind us. All of this shapes how we move and interact with the world around us. In this lesson we will talk about why dance cannot be separated from everyday life, and why change often begins not with trying to move better, but with learning to notice what is happening right now.

2.title: Between two legs
2.description: In tango we often get used to transferring weight quickly from one leg to the other. As a result, movement becomes predictable, and many decisions are made automatically. In this lesson I suggest exploring the space between two supports and looking at how having a choice affects the quality of movement, speed, and possibilities for improvisation.

3.title: One step — three characters
3.description: Many dancers get used to using the same way of moving and over time stop noticing that the same step can have a completely different character. In this lesson we explore three ways of organizing movement and look at how they affect the feeling of the step, the quality of movement, and possibilities for adaptation in the dance.

4.title: Not creating, but guiding
4.description: In interaction the question often arises: who is responsible for the movement? Should the leader create every action, or can part of the movement happen on its own? In this lesson we explore one possible view of interaction in the couple. Using the musical beat as the basis for movement, we will look at how the leader can avoid creating movement from scratch and instead guide a process that is already underway.

5.title: Who is responsible for the turn?
5.description: Often the follower tries to turn on her own, while the leader assumes the turn should already be happening by itself. As a result both sides take on only part of the responsibility, and the interaction becomes less clear. In this lesson we will conduct an unusual experiment and temporarily hand full responsibility for the pivot to the leader, in order to look afresh at the process of leading and following.

6.title: When connection becomes visible
6.description: Interaction in the couple is often perceived as something invisible. We talk about connection, contact, and communication, but we cannot always clearly see what is happening between two people during movement. In this lesson we will use a simple external reference that will help us look anew at how interaction is organized and explore the connection between two bodies in motion.

7.title: Opening space
7.description: Sometimes leading is perceived as an attempt to move the partner from one point to another. But what if we look at this process differently? In this lesson we will explore interaction through the space between partners and observe how small changes of direction can create new possibilities for movement.

8.title: The power of the weak beat
8.description: Most dancers get used to starting movement on the strong beat of the music. Gradually this becomes so habitual that weak beats begin to be perceived only as the interval between important events. In this lesson we explore the weak beat as a new reference for movement and look at how changing the habitual point of entry into the music can affect the character of the dance, the quality of movement, and musicality.

9.title: Posture without effort
9.description: Often work on posture turns into a constant attempt to hold something in place, straighten, or control. Over time this leads to extra tension and the feeling that good posture requires constant effort. In this lesson we explore a different approach. Instead of trying to fix the body we will use imagination as a tool for organizing movement and look at how different images affect the quality of posture and movement.

10.title: Living embraces
10.description: Very often, striving to maintain beautiful posture and stable embraces, we gradually begin to fix the shoulders, shoulder blades, and upper body. Over time the embrace becomes less mobile, and the interaction loses part of its natural quality. In this lesson we explore how small changes in how the shoulder girdle is organized can affect the quality of the embrace, interaction in the couple, and the feeling of movement.

11.title: More than a step
11.description: Often the strong beat of the music is automatically associated with a step. Over time this connection becomes so habitual that we stop noticing other possibilities for interacting with the music. In this lesson we will use the strong beat as a reference and explore what other actions can happen in that moment. This approach helps expand musical thinking and make the dance more varied.

12.title: Not only face to face
12.description: In partner dances the idea often arises that partners must constantly remain strictly face to face. Over time this turns into a habit that begins to limit the perception of space and possibilities for movement. In this lesson we will explore the giro in different mutual positions and look at how changing the partners' placement affects technique, interaction, and variability.

13.title: Space between the beats
13.description: Often we try to make every step equally important, expressive, and high in quality. Over time movement begins to repeat with the same character, and the space between musical accents goes unnoticed. In this lesson we will explore the contrast between accent and soft continuation of movement, in order to better feel time, space, and the musical structure of the dance.

14.title: Who moves around whom?
14.description: Often the same roles in movement repeat again and again. The leader leads. The follower goes around. The same trajectories gradually become habitual and begin to be perceived as the only possible ones. In this lesson we will explore different ways of organizing movement and look at how the dance changes when the very principle of who moves around whom changes.

15.title: Feeling the free leg
15.description: Very often during the dance all attention is focused on the standing leg, weight transfer, and direction of movement. Meanwhile the free leg begins to be perceived as something secondary, although it often becomes an important part of interaction within the couple. In this lesson we will explore how a state of readiness for movement helps you feel the partner's free leg better and opens new possibilities for leading, interaction, and organizing movement.

16.title: New music for a familiar movement
16.description: Often certain movements gradually begin to be associated with a certain rhythm. Over time this connection becomes so habitual that movement and the rhythmic pattern begin to be perceived as a single whole. In this lesson we will explore what happens when a familiar movement receives a new rhythmic organization. This approach helps develop musicality, expand variability, and notice new possibilities within movements you already know.

17.title: Four speeds of time
17.description: Very often fast rhythmic patterns seem difficult and inaccessible. Yet the problem is far from always related to the speed of movement. Much more often we simply lack experience perceiving time at different levels. In this lesson we will explore four speeds of time and observe how our perception of the music changes when the density of the count changes. This approach helps you better understand musical structure and gradually prepares us for working with syncopation.

18.title: Bringing it all together
18.description: Over the course of this journey we will become acquainted with different ideas, observations, and ways of exploring movement. In this lesson we will bring all the main principles together and look at them as parts of one system. We will return to ideas we already know and see how they begin to support and complement each other in the dance.

19.title: Every step is a choice
19.description: In this lesson we will continue to explore the Giro — a movement in which the follower most often moves around the leader and which opens a huge number of possibilities for interaction, musicality, and variability. Very often familiar movements begin to be perceived as a fixed sequence of steps. Over time the feeling arises that each step is already predetermined and all that remains is to execute it. We will look at how small changes of direction within each step of the Giro can affect interaction, the quality of rotation, and possibilities for improvisation.

20.title: The invisible connection
20.description: Usually we perceive the movement of arms and legs as separate processes. Because of this some possibilities for interaction remain unnoticed, and movement becomes more fragmented. In this lesson we will explore connections within the body and look at how changing one part can affect the movement of another. This approach helps make interaction clearer and movement more connected and fluid.

21.title: Support first
21.description: Often all attention is directed at the movement itself. We think about where to go, how to take a step, or how to organize interaction. Meanwhile what makes movement freer and more stable often goes unnoticed. In this lesson we will explore how searching for support affects the quality of movement and interaction. We will look at how the sensation of support helps create more freedom, lightness, and clarity both in your own movement and in working with your partner.

22.title: The moment of the fourth speed
22.description: In the previous lesson we explored four speeds of time and became acquainted with the fastest of them. Now it is time to use it in movement. In this lesson we will explore how a brief shift to the fourth speed can change the character of movement, musicality, and interaction in the couple. We will see that syncopation is not a separate mode of dancing, but one way to temporarily change the density of movement within the music.

23.title: Following the free side
23.description: Often movement begins with effort. We get used to pushing off from the standing leg, transferring weight, and creating impulse for the next step. In this lesson we will try to explore a different approach and look at what happens when movement begins to be organized through the free side of the body. This approach helps make movement softer, more connected, and more sensitive to interaction.

24.title: Another perspective
24.description: Very often we explore movement only while standing on our feet. Over time this habit begins to limit our perception and makes some connections within the body less noticeable. In this lesson we will change the habitual conditions for exploring movement and look at how working in a new position helps you better feel the relationship between the pelvis, legs, torso, and movement as a whole.
